newsitem.title: USA: Anti-depressant drugs found not to harm fetus.
newsitem.headline: Anti-depressant drugs found not to harm fetus.

text.p: Babies whose mothers took common depression-fighting medicines during pregnancy show no evidence of harm when the children grow to pre-school age, a study to be published on Thursday concluded.
The findings in the New England Journal of Medicine should be comforting news to women who have taken -- or are taking -- Prozac or tricyclic antidepressant drugs during their pregnancy.

"Until now, physicians have not had the information they need to reassure women that exposure to these drugs during the first trimester, or continuous use during pregnancy, is safe," Dr. Gideon Koren of the Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto said in a statement.
"As a result, women very often discontinued needed drug treatment, risking severe illness or even suicide attempts," he said.

Koren and other researchers at the hospital looked at the offspring of 80 mothers who took some form of tricyclic drug during pregnancy, 55 children whose mothers had gotten Prozac, and 84 children of women who had gotten another type of medicine, such as penicillin, that does not harm a fetus.
The newborns were tracked for up to seven years.

When they compared the results among the three groups, "We found there was no difference between children who were exposed to the drugs and those who weren't," psychologist Joanne Rovert, another member of the team, said in a news release.

Specifically, they found no significant difference in the average IQ scores or language test scores, or "in temperament, mood, arousability, activity level, distractibility, or behavior problems in the three groups of children," the researchers concluded.
It also made no difference whether a woman had taken one of the depression-fighting drugs throughout her pregnancy, or just at the beginning.

About 8 to 20 percent of women suffer from depression at some time in their lives, usually during their childbearing years. In addition, about half of all pregnancies are unplanned, which means the fetus is often exposed to the mother's medications before the woman knows she is pregnant.
Prozac, the most commonly used depression-fighting drug in the United States, is also known by its generic name fluoxetine. It is sold by Eli Lilly and Co.

Past studies of the effects of such drugs on the fetus have been open for debate because they sometimes did not take into consideration factors such as cigarette consumption, alcohol use, or medical problems of the mother.

Last October, a team led by Christina Chambers of the University of California, San Diego, reported that their study of 482 women showed that Prozac may cause several minor infant abnormalities if it is taken during pregnancy.

But that finding was greeted with skepticism because earlier studies had failed to find a problem. In addition, other factors such as the way women were selected for the study or other medicines they were taking might explain the result.
The researchers did not find a link between the drug and any particular type of abnormality, which usually happens if a drug causes birth defects.
